title: Valid Palindrome II
directAnswer: Walk two pointers inward checking for a palindrome. At the first mismatch you get exactly one delete — so greedily try both: skip the left char OR skip the right char, and return true if either remaining substring is a palindrome. O(n) time, O(1) space.

remember.pattern: Two pointers + one greedy branch on first mismatch
rules: On the **first mismatch**, branch: verify `s[lo+1..hi]` OR `s[lo..hi-1]` — you have exactly **one** delete to spend.
If the pointers cross with no mismatch, it's **already a palindrome** → return true without using the delete.
The greedy branch is **provably complete**: the deleted char must be one of the two mismatched ends, never an inner char.
Write a clean `isPalindrome(lo, hi)` helper — both branches reuse it on a fixed range, so it must take explicit bounds.
Don't recurse for **two** deletes — that's a different (harder) problem. One mismatch, one branch, done.
whenToUse: Checking palindrome / symmetry with **at most one** edit (delete) allowed
Two pointers from the ends, deciding what to do at the first conflict
You can prove the only viable fix involves the **boundary** elements
Need O(1) space — no copying substrings
antiSignals: Up to **k** deletes allowed → DP / recursion (Valid Palindrome III, LCS-style)
Insertions/replacements allowed too → edit-distance DP, not greedy
No edit budget at all → plain palindrome check (Valid Palindrome I)
Mismatch could be fixed by an **interior** delete → greedy boundary branch is wrong
remember.takeaway: With one allowed delete, the fix must be at the boundary, so you only ever branch once: skip left or skip right and re-verify. Two pointers + a single greedy fork keeps it O(n)/O(1) — recognise this whenever an 'almost palindrome' has a tiny edit budget.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you realize the single delete forces the fix to be one of the two mismatched boundary characters — so you branch exactly once instead of exploring every deletion. Also whether you factor out a bounded palindrome helper cleanly.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Trying to be clever about *which* side to delete with a heuristic (e.g. always delete the side with the 'wrong' char) instead of just trying both, or restarting the whole scan after a delete and blowing up to O(n²) needlessly via substring copies.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Prove the greedy is complete: 'at a mismatch s[lo] != s[hi], a single delete can only remove s[lo] or s[hi] — deleting any interior char leaves the boundary mismatch unfixed. So checking both branches is exhaustive.'

problemStatement:
Given a string `s`, return `true` if `s` can be a palindrome after deleting **at most one** character from it.

A palindrome reads the same forward and backward. Deleting at most one character means you may delete zero or one character.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters only
understanding: Standard palindrome check, but you're allowed a single 'mulligan': if exactly one pair of characters refuses to match, you may delete one of the two offenders and the rest must form a palindrome. Zero deletes (already a palindrome) is also valid.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the delete budget exactly one, or at most one?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: At most one. An already-valid palindrome must return true without spending the delete.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are we deleting or replacing/inserting?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Deleting only. That's why the fix is always 'skip a boundary char' — replacement or insertion would change the algorithm to edit-distance DP.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could the answer require deleting an interior character?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. The first mismatch is at the boundary; a single delete that fixes it must remove one of those two boundary chars. That's what makes the greedy branch complete.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What characters and what size?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Lowercase letters, up to 10⁵ chars. So I want O(n) — no quadratic substring rebuilding.

Mismatch at a/c. Neither "bc" nor "ab" is a palindrome — one delete isn't enough.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Try Every Deletion
approaches.whenToMention: Mention to anchor the progression, then note the redundant rescans make it O(n²) and motivate the greedy.
hints: If you're allowed to delete one character, what's the most direct way to test the claim?
For each index i, build the string with s[i] removed, then check if that's a palindrome. Also check the original (zero deletes).
That's n+1 palindrome checks, each O(n), and each rebuilt string costs O(n) memory. Correct, but wasteful — most deletions are obviously pointless.
approaches.complexityReasoning: n+1 candidate strings × O(n) palindrome check = O(n²) time; each rebuilt string is O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
The literal reading: 'delete at most one character' becomes 'try deleting each character (and also deleting none), and see if any result is a palindrome.'

**Why it's the natural baseline.** It mirrors the problem statement one-to-one — enumerate every allowed move and test the goal. No insight required, which is exactly why it's worth stating before optimizing.

**Why it's wasteful.** Almost every deletion is irrelevant. If `s[lo]` already equals `s[hi]` at the matching positions, deleting some character buried in the middle can't possibly help — yet brute force still rebuilds the whole string and rescans it. For `n = 10⁵`, `O(n²)` is ~10¹⁰ operations: a hard time-limit failure.

**The key realization it leads to.** When you watch brute force run, you notice the *only* deletions that ever matter are at the place where a plain palindrome check first breaks. That observation is what collapses `n+1` candidate scans into a single forked check — the greedy approach below.
approaches.insight: Brute force exposes the waste: you rescan the entire string for deletions that can't affect a mismatch you haven't even reached yet. The fix only ever needs to happen at the first conflict — which is the seed of the greedy solution.

dryRun.intro: Try deleting each index plus the no-delete case; stop at the first candidate that's a palindrome.

java.explanation: Rebuild the string without index i — this O(n) copy per iteration is the source of the O(n²).
Any single deletion that yields a palindrome proves the answer.

python.explanation: String slice removing index i; O(n) per iteration.
Reverse-compare to test palindrome — also O(n).

pitfalls: Forgetting the zero-delete case — an already-valid palindrome must return true.
Rebuilding substrings inside the loop — O(n²) time and O(n) space, too slow for 10⁵.
Assuming only one deletion 'side' matters without proof — here you brute everything, which hides the real insight.

approaches.name: Two Pointers + Greedy One-Delete Branch (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Lead with the completeness proof: 'the fix must be one of the two mismatched boundary chars'.
hints: Run a normal palindrome check with two pointers. What's the earliest moment you actually need your one delete?
At the first mismatch s[lo] != s[hi], a single delete can only remove s[lo] or s[hi] — deleting anything in between leaves the boundary broken.
So return isPalindrome(lo+1, hi) || isPalindrome(lo, hi-1). Use a helper that checks a fixed [lo, hi] range so no substrings are copied.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The outer scan is O(n). At most one mismatch triggers a single helper call that scans at most the remaining range — also O(n). Total O(n). Only integer indices → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
March `lo` from the left and `hi` from the right. While `s[lo] == s[hi]`, step both inward. If the pointers cross without conflict, the string was already a palindrome — return true with the delete unused. The interesting case is the **first** mismatch.

**Why a single greedy branch is exhaustive.** At the first mismatch we have `s[lo] != s[hi]`, and everything outside `[lo, hi]` already matched as a mirror. Our one delete has to make `[lo, hi]` palindromic. Could the deleted character be some interior char `s[k]` with `lo < k < hi`? No — removing an interior char leaves `s[lo]` and `s[hi]` still sitting at the boundary, still unequal, so the range still fails. **The only deletions that can possibly fix a boundary mismatch are deleting `s[lo]` or deleting `s[hi]`.** That's why we check exactly two sub-ranges — `[lo+1, hi]` and `[lo, hi-1]` — and ORing them is provably complete, not a heuristic.

**Why we don't pick a side cleverly.** A tempting bug is to decide *which* end to delete based on, say, comparing `s[lo+1]` with `s[hi]`. Such heuristics break on strings like `"cupucu"` where local context misleads. Trying *both* branches costs nothing asymptotically (each is a linear scan of a shrinking range) and is bulletproof. Simplicity wins here.

**Why the helper takes explicit bounds.** Both branches re-verify a *fixed sub-range* of the original string. If the helper rebuilt substrings we'd be back to O(n) copies; instead it walks indices in place, so the whole algorithm stays O(1) space. This is the difference between the optimal and the brute force — same idea, no allocation.

**Why the budget is spent at most once.** After the first mismatch we either succeed (return true) or fail (return false) — we never continue the outer loop. That's the structural reason this solves the *one*-delete problem specifically; extending to k deletes would require recursion or DP and a fundamentally different shape.
approaches.insight: A bounded edit budget localizes the decision: with one delete, the fix is pinned to the first boundary conflict, so you fork exactly once. Generalize the mental model — 'how big is the edit budget?' decides whether you greedily branch (k=1) or fall back to DP (k>1). The bounded-range palindrome helper is the reusable primitive.

pitfalls: Choosing which side to delete by a heuristic instead of trying both — fails on adversarial inputs.
Making the helper rebuild substrings — reintroduces O(n) space and can push time toward O(n²).
Continuing the outer loop after a mismatch instead of returning — that would allow more than one delete.
Forgetting the no-mismatch case returns true (zero deletes is allowed).

commonMistakes: Using a heuristic to pick the delete side instead of trying both branches.
Rebuilding substrings for each candidate deletion — O(n²) time, O(n) space.
Forgetting that an already-valid palindrome (zero deletes) must return true.
Letting the algorithm spend more than one delete by continuing the scan.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Heuristic side-picking instead of trying both
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Deciding which char to delete from local comparisons fails on inputs where the wrong local choice is misleading. Trying both branches is free asymptotically and always correct.
commonMistakesDetailed.good: return is_palindrome(lo + 1, hi) or is_palindrome(lo, hi - 1)

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Substring copies in the helper
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Slicing/concatenating to check a sub-range turns each verification into an O(n) allocation, defeating the O(1)-space goal and risking O(n²) time.
commonMistakesDetailed.good: boolean ok = isPalindrome(s, lo + 1, hi);  // checks range in place

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Spending more than one delete
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you 'skip' a char and then keep looping the outer pointers, a second mismatch could trigger a second skip — solving a different problem.
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if s[lo] != s[hi]:
    return is_palindrome(lo + 1, hi) or is_palindrome(lo, hi - 1)
